parsed_answer.content: Understanding algorithm selection for sorting—specifically balancing merge sort, quick sort, counting sort, and radix sort—is a hallmark of a senior Java engineer. When architecting high-throughput systems processing millions of records, choosing the wrong algorithm directly impacts CPU cache locality, branch prediction, and garbage collection pressure. Merge sort provides a stable divide-and-conquer strategy guaranteeing O(N log N) worst-case performance, making it the bedrock for objects requiring stable ordering or external sorting of massive datasets exceeding RAM capacity. Quick sort relies on in-place partitioning with an average-case O(N log N) runtime, which, due to its exceptional cache-line efficiency, typically outperforms merge sort in raw speed for primitive arrays, despite a degraded O(N^2) worst case when partitioned poorly. Counting sort and radix sort deviate entirely from comparison-based boundaries, offering O(N) linear-time execution under specific constraints. Counting sort acts as an integer distribution sort ideal for small, bounded keys, while radix sort processes keys digit-by-digit (or byte-by-byte), serving as the ultimate tool for fixed-length strings or dense integer primitives where the key space is structured.

items: Merge sort allocates auxiliary arrays during the merge phase, which can trigger significant Minor GC overhead if executed repeatedly in tight loops over large object graphs; Java's TimSort (used in Arrays.sort for objects) optimizes this by merging existing run segments.

Quick sort performance heavily depends on pivot selection. Dual-pivot strategies (used in java.util.Arrays.sort for primitives) partition the array into three parts, mitigating worst-case quadratic behavior on patterned or duplicate-heavy data.

Counting sort trades space for time by allocating an auxiliary frequency array of size K (the range of input values). It completely bypasses CPU branch mispredictions inherent in comparison sorts, making it exceptionally fast for narrow value ranges.

Radix sort relies on a stable inner sort (typically counting sort) applied across successive digit positions from least significant to most significant (LSD) or vice versa (MSD), scaling linearly with the key length W.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of blindly using standard library sorts in performance-critical microservices. While Arrays.sort() intelligently switches between Dual-Pivot Quicksort for primitives and TimSort for objects, misuse of object sorting on large wrapper object arrays (e.g., Integer[] instead of int[]) creates massive memory fragmentation and pointer-chasing overhead. For non-comparison sorts like counting and radix, always validate that your key space K is tightly bound; otherwise, you risk catastrophic OutOfMemoryError exceptions due to massive frequency table allocations.
